extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter on the nature of reason, concepts, judgment, and the role and limits of logic; explains concept-formation, relations among concepts (spheres), origin of logical rules, and the distinction between rational knowledge and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason has one function
rubrics_metrics.description: So also the reason has one function; and from it all the manifestations of reason we have mentioned, which distinguish the life of man from that of the brutes, may easily be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single function of reason underlies such manifestations as control of the emotions and passions, capacity for drawing conclusions, formulating general principles (even a priori), language, planned co-operation, civilisation, science, and the communication of truth and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding's sole function
rubrics_metrics.description: The understanding has only one function—immediate knowledge of the relation of cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception of the real world, common sense, sagacity, and inventiveness are seen as manifestations of this single function; the passage stresses the fundamental and unitary role of the understanding in causal apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts are a distinct class of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts form a distinct class of ideas, existing only in the mind of man, and entirely different from the ideas of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concepts cannot be presented in perception and therefore cannot be verified directly by external experience; they are only thought, not perceived. Language communicates these abstract conceptions; this explains why lower animals cannot learn or comprehend human language in the conceptual sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts are 'ideas of ideas' with a ground relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection is the necessary copy or repetition of the originally presented world of perception... concepts may quite properly be called ideas of ideas, and the whole nature of the abstract idea is simply and solely its relation to another idea, which is its ground of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chain of grounds of knowledge for abstract concepts must terminate in a concept grounded in perception; the principle of sufficient reason takes a special form for concepts as relations to their grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracta vs. Concreta distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Those concepts which are not immediately related to the world of perception have been called abstracta, and those which have their ground immediately in the world of perception have been called concreta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of abstracta: 'relation', 'virtue', 'investigation'; examples of (loosely called) concreta: 'man', 'stone', 'horse'. The text notes the terminology is loose because even 'concreta' are abstract ideas, not perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality is essential to a concept (not merely derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not... an essential characteristic of a concept that it should contain much under it... This characteristic arises merely as derived and secondary; a concept may be abstract and general even if only one real object corresponds to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generality (non-determination of the particular) belongs to the concept as an abstract idea; example: the conception of a particular town known only from geography may be applicable to other towns differing in respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts possess extension or sphere and overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Every concept... has what is called extension or sphere... the sphere of one concept has something in common with the sphere of other concepts; the recognition of this relation is called judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representing these spheres pictorially (lines, squares, Euler circles) helps make the a priori relations of concepts plain in perception and grounds the doctrine of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five basic relations of concept-spheres
rubrics_metrics.description:
(1) The spheres of two concepts coincide (convertible).
(2) The sphere of one concept includes that of the other.
(3) A sphere includes two or more spheres which exclude each other and fill it.
(4) Two spheres include each a part of the other (overlap).
(5) Two spheres lie in a third, but do not fill it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five cases exhaust the possible relations of concept-spheres and are the basis for conversion, contraposition, equipollence, disjunction, and other features of judgment and syllogistic theory; the text gives biological and geometric examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of judgment and syllogism derives from sphere combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: To these cases all combinations of concepts may be referred, and from them the entire doctrine of the judgment, its conversion, contraposition, equipollence, disjunction... may be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the schematism of concepts (diagrammatic spheres) one can deduce syllogistic rules by construction; this provides the foundation for the theory of judgment and the syllogism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic's limited practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is never of practical use, but has only a theoretical interest for philosophy... It is nothing more than the knowledge in the abstract of what every one knows in the concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic is useful like thorough-bass for composition—valuable theoretically but not necessary for correct practice; its practical use is largely confined to exposing intentional fallacies in debate by technical names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic as paraphrase of the principle of sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is only a paraphrase of this principle, and, more exactly, only of that exemplification of it in which the ground that gives truth to the judgment is neither empirical nor metaphysical, but logical or metalogical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exposition of logic should focus on the nature of reason and the principle of sufficient reason of knowing rather than on mere practical rules; metalogical laws related to this principle must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four metalogical principles as pure rational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no absolutely pure rational knowledge except the four principles to which I have attributed metalogical truth; the principles of identity, contradiction, excluded middle, and sufficient reason of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the rest of logic presupposes relations and combinations of spheres of concepts; these four are presented as the sole absolutely pure instances of rational knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rational knowledge (wissen)
rubrics_metrics.description: To know rationally (wissen) means to have in the power of the mind, and capable of being reproduced at will, such judgments as have their sufficient ground of knowledge in something outside themselves, i.e., are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational knowledge is abstract cognition and the permanent possession in concepts of what has been known otherwise; lower animals do not 'rationally know' though they have perception, memory, and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling as the negative opposite of rational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept which the word feeling denotes has merely a negative content, which is this, that something which is present in consciousness, is not a concept, is not abstract rational knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sphere of 'feeling' includes diverse phenomena (religious feeling, sensual pleasure, moral feeling, bodily sensations, aesthetic feeling, etc.); the author suggests using a separate term (empfindung) for bodily feeling to reduce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistry traced to manipulation of overlapping concept-spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of sophistry lies in casting only a superficial glance at the relations of the spheres of the concepts, and then manipulating these relations to suit our purposes... treating a partially overlapping sphere as if it lay entirely within one or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophists exploit overlapping conceptual spheres by highlighting only the containment relation that suits their aim and concealing others; example: subsuming 'passion' under different larger concepts (greatest force vs. irrational) to arrive at desired conclusions.
